mappings.note: The condition for choosing fractional over simple distillation -- a small boiling-point difference. LO-10's 'states when each is the appropriate method' is written for exactly this pair-wise choice.

Refinery application of fractional distillation, justified by the small boiling-point gaps between crude fractions. LO-10. Same outcome as the MCQ on petroleum, which is honest: the frame gives fractional distillation no separate outcome from simple distillation.
What makes ink components travel at different rates -- their differing interaction with solvent and paper, which is LO-11's principle clause.
Locates the separation on the paper itself as the solvent rises -- the stationary-phase half of LO-11's principle, distinct from the preceding item which asks what drives the differential movement.

POOR FIT. Pure etymology -- chroma plus graphein. LO-11 is cited only because it is the sole chromatography code; the outcome is about the principle and solvent choice, and no outcome in curriculum 82 covers terminology origins.
Names the separating funnel for an immiscible pair -- the selection half of LO-11, in its most literal form.
Why the oil is on top: lower density. The justification half of LO-11, matching the earlier which-layer-is-at-the-bottom MCQ from the opposite end.
Names sublimation for the solid-to-vapour transition. LO-12's first clause; deposition is not asked about here.
Camphor and dry ice share sublimation. LO-12. It tests which substances are sublimable, which is the property that makes the technique applicable in LO-12's second clause.
What an alloy is made of, answered as a homogeneous mixture of metals or a metal and a non-metal. LO-6 names alloys among the everyday mixtures to classify, and the homogeneity claim is its core.

Defines a suspension by large undissolved particles held through the medium -- LO-14's three-way distinction seen from the suspension side. LO-6 would apply if the wanted answer were simply 'heterogeneous', but the assessed content is the particle behaviour.
Principle of centrifugation. LO-13 is the only outcome naming it. Honestly the same code as the MCQ on the same principle -- the frame does not separate mechanism from selection for centrifugation.
Where coagulation is used in daily life, answered with water purification of fine muddy impurities -- LO-13's exact scenario, fine particles that filtration cannot hold.
The function of alum specifically: clumping fine mud into settleable aggregates. LO-13's coagulation clause, narrower than the preceding item which asks for the use case.
Suspension versus true solution stated explicitly in nanometres -- LO-14's 'uses particle size to distinguish'. The question itself says 'based on particle size', which fixes the outcome.
Defines the dispersed phase against the dispersion medium -- the naming clause of LO-15. No light test and no size band, so neither LO-14 nor the Tyndall half is engaged.
Why the beam is visible: scattering by colloidal particles. LO-15's demonstration clause, asked as a why rather than as an observation.
POOR FIT. The answer is a person's name, John Tyndall. LO-15 is cited as the only code mentioning the Tyndall effect, but no outcome in this frame covers history-of-science or attribution recall.

An everyday emulsion example with both phases liquid -- LO-15's 'recognising an emulsion as a liquid colloid'. Milk recurs across this chapter, but here it is the emulsion clause and not the Tyndall one.

Explains the Tyndall effect (LO-15), then contrasts milk with salt water, which can only be done with the 1-1000 nm versus sub-1 nm size bands (LO-14). Same two-code rule used on the other Tyndall items where the size figure is the discriminator.
Homogeneous versus heterogeneous on composition and visible boundaries -- LO-6's 'by observation' clause at three-mark length. No technique and no size threshold.
Draws the separating funnel setup and states the density principle for mustard oil and water -- both halves of LO-11, selection and justification, in one item.

Defines sublimation and deposition together and then names a solid mixture separable by it -- LO-12 end to end. This is the fullest single item on that outcome; the shorter LO-12 items each take only one clause.

Crystallisation versus evaporation to dryness on purity grounds -- LO-9's principle. The long-form twin of the earlier MCQ on the same comparison; both honestly land on LO-9 because purity of crystals has no other home.
Colloid versus suspension on size and on settling -- both of LO-14's clauses, and only those two. No Tyndall test is invoked, which keeps it off LO-15.
